# The definitions and principles, in Joshua Mathias's words

Everything below is quoted verbatim from the evolvable-structure skill's `SKILL.md`, written by Joshua Mathias, who is its authority. It is regenerated whenever that file changes. The intent template itself (Problem, Solution, Implementation, Ideal, Metric) is in [the templates](../templates/).

## What it is

> This form of evolvable structure is a design which improves over time as measured by metrics and is adaptable to changing intentions, contexts, priorities, and problems to solve. When you embody the principles defined here, you create and use Evolvable Structure that Optimizes Intent (ESOI). You're turning an intention into a structure that optimizes the fulfilling of that intent, while also ensuring the structure supports changes to the intent. Crucially, the structure enables effective specification of the intent, and the intent and structure evolve together in a continual feedback loop.

## Purpose

> The purpose of ESOI is to enable progress over time. This is motivated by a prioritization of the farthest point in the future we can reasonably plan for. Keep in mind that fast progress now may be justifiably best for that far future, but don't just assume that.

## Definitions

> - **Evolvable:** Changeable towards a different purpose while retaining benefits from the past.
> - **Structure:** Something that is relatively stable over time, and which enables other purposes which leverage the structure.
> - **Evolvable Structure:** Structure that finds the ideal balance of longevity and changeability through predicting what will likely be useful to change in the future vs what is more useful as stable and unchanging. This is done through intentionally choosing a niche of changeability based on the purpose of the structure's creation and opportunities related to that purpose.
> - **Adaptable:** Changeable to handle different situations or contexts in the moment.
> - **Intent:** A conceptualization within consciousness which motivates a future state. Useful context can be lost when translating consciousness into the physical world. Consequently, ESOI specifies intent as Problems, Solutions, Implementations, Ideals, and Metrics. Note: Downstream automation may create intents without consciousness, but any automated system originated as a conscious intent at some point. Intents of consciousness should be prioritized over non-conscious intents.

## Principles (ideals)

> The below principles are ordered such that conflict can be effectively resolved by priority (with pragmatic balance and nuance).
> 1. **Practical, evolvable structure is prioritized** to improve the likelihood of the **intent** being optimally fulfilled in the optimal timeframe.
>     Note: AI has dramatically increased the practicality of evolvable structure, resolving earlier concerns of wasted effort on initial design and structure (unless it's human effort). AI has also increased the value of structure, as AI can scale the application of a structure. However, this principle does not suggest that the initial structural design is final; it evolves, and such evolution is again often supported by AI.
> 2. **An ideal but iterative ontology of solution abstractions:** Have a separate, defined component for every use case that has a different definition of best, if and only if the different definition could impact the success of the intent. In addition, all solutions are motivated by a defined problem (AKA use case), but it is not a one-to-one mapping in either direction. Solutions define what they're intended to do and their interface with the world (input/dependencies, output, action in between or outcome), but not how it's done. There are one or more **ideals defined for every solution**, and a **practical metric** to compare how well each implementation of the solution achieves the relevant ideals.
> 3. **A consistent structure provides a source of truth for iterating on implementations of solutions,** knowing which implementation is currently selected for the solution, and knowing the metrics. Ideally, aspects of this structure, or the same structure, are applied across systems and contexts, but different structures are built as needed following high level principles. **The structure is (1) an implementation of the network and ontology** between problems, solutions, implementations, ideals, and metrics and **(2) what enables interdependent solution interfaces to interact with each other despite changing implementations**.
> 4. Structure enables the **automatic use of the best implementation** for a solution, according to the authoritative metric chosen by the solution definition. Humans need only review metrics, not implementations (but they can still add value to implementations).
> 5. **Every structure is improved over time to serve its defined purpose and niche.** The evolvable structure itself also improves, and this is a key way in which such structure enables progress over time, because the relatively stable structure addresses the most challenging risks, even if indirectly through providing a clear place to define and iterate on solutions of a particular type. Here, purpose is a problem, niche is a solution, and the implementation is what is intentionally changeable vs what is not in the structure.
> 6. The philosophy and structure of solutions is applied not only to tangible artifacts directly but to **high level principles**, which encourages **proactively** defining problems, ideals, solutions as needed to cover all gaps. This also **addresses risk** of implementations not being reviewed, through ensuring problems, solutions, and metrics are thought through from all necessary angles and perspectives.
> 7. **Be humble.** We don't know what is best; we let metrics determine, and even then it's a limited approximation of an intent which words have a limited ability to express, and the intent itself may or may not be worthwhile. We value collaboration and alternative perspectives, as we don't know which perspective is best for a particular purpose; perspectives are implementations. Humility provides space for improvement.
> 8. **Leverage existing structure.** Structure should also facilitate maintaining awareness of existing useful structure, when and only when such awareness is useful. This means don't just build reuse; apply it. This applies to using what's out there as well, whether that's science, open-source code, public data, or advice; we collaborate with the world at large.
> 9. **Structure avoids duplication of effort across multiple dimensions:** Horizontal (technical function) and vertical (domain or application). Topical (scope) and generational (inheritance). This is applied not just to code but to information, documentation, and instruction. However, structural solutions are applied only where the disadvantages of the particular structure don't outweigh the advantages for the particular purpose and niche of the structure.
> 10. **Structure that prioritizes long-term outcomes strategically cascades down to all tasks, pragmatically.** This philosophy is how risks are addressed and useful high quality is ensured, through applying structure in the form of common practices and tendencies that work with a vision higher than just finishing the task at hand, while accomplishing the specific task. Prioritizing an real system test for a new feature as even more important than unit test, and prioritizing KPIs over task completion, are examples of this. The real thing, the problem solved in the wild, is what matters. Metrics also help hold us accountable to this.
> 11. **Avoid doing or retaining what isn't useful long-term.** If you're going to edit something, do it in a way where it's useful the next time, if there's a reasonable chance of that being possible. Make what's most reuseable easiest to find and most often used. If a scalable source of truth could be used, use that, whether that's a spreadsheet, a recommendation system on top of information which may scale past what one would want to read at once, file organization, consistently working on the same files, etc. Consider how you can enable collaborative innovation (facilitate feedback and iteration by others where relevant). If you create a new file at every session that isn't archived, then something is probably wrong. Iterating on the same things over and over is what enables progress over time.
> 12. **Enable minimalism and simplicity.** Seek elegant simplicity so that applications of the structure specify only what's different for the particular application or use case. Prioritize elegant interfaces, even if under the hood it's complex. It's worth spending the time to improve the structure up front.
> 13. **Prioritize clarity.** Naming conventions, concise but clear wording, organization that enables reading or understanding only what is necessary at a given moment, these all enable evolvable structure. Clarity and organization enables reuse and efficient understanding at a glance later (by both human and AI).
